props.title: Les Yeux Sans Visage

sections.content: Les Yeux Sans Visage revolutionized horror by blending poetic beauty with medical terror. Director Georges Franju crafted a haunting tale of Dr. Génessier's obsessive quest to restore his daughter Christiane's disfigured face through gruesome skin grafts. The film's influence echoes through later works like The Skin I Live In (2011) and The Face of Another (1966), establishing a uniquely European approach to body horror that prioritizes psychological dread over gore. Edith Scob's performance behind the blank white mask became an iconic image, later referenced in Halloween (1978) and Drive (2011).

sections.content: The film's surgical scenes shocked 1960s audiences while establishing a new vocabulary for medical horror. Later films like Dead Ringers (1988) and The Human Centipede (2009) would push surgical horror to extremes, but none matched Franju's ability to make beauty and terror dance so elegantly together. The film's exploration of identity through facial disfigurement influenced everything from Phantom of the Paradise (1974) to Face/Off (1997).

Beyond horror, Les Yeux Sans Visage pioneered themes of body modification and identity that resonate through art cinema. Persona (1966) borrowed its mask imagery, while Holy Motors (2012) directly homaged Edith Scob's iconic look. The film's influence on fashion and music videos continues today, with artists like Lady Gaga referencing its clinical-yet-ethereal aesthetic. SUBHEAD: Legacy in Modern Cinema

sections.content: Modern filmmakers continue drawing from Franju's masterpiece. Goodnight Mommy (2014) uses facial bandages to create similar uncertainty about identity, while Under the Skin (2013) echoes the film's combination of beauty and body horror. The surgical precision and moral ambiguity of The Human Centipede (2009) owes a clear debt to Dr. Génessier's methodical madness.
